Churned customers did file more support tickets on average over the last 90 days than customers who stayed, but only a little more. I computed this across all 1,200 customers, using `churned_next_month` to split them. I'm assuming 1 means the customer churned the following month. I'd call the gap modest. I haven't tested whether it's more than chance, and it doesn't show that tickets cause churn. What are you hoping to do with this? For example, are you checking whether support load is an early warning sign of churn, or looking at how well support is working? That decides whether I give you exact figures in a small table, break them down by plan or segment, or go further.

kind of the first one? my manager wants the senior agents to take the subscribers most likely to leave. only about 500 a month fit in that queue, so i need some way to pick them. i was thinking the averages would work for that?

Averages describe the two groups, not individual customers, so they can't pick 500 people on their own. The gap you saw is small. Most customers have about the same number of tickets whether they leave or stay, so tickets alone won't tell you who is about to go. What your manager needs is a ranking: a score for each subscriber's chance of leaving, built from everything in the table (plan, tenure, spend, segment, city and tickets). You would then hand the top 500 to the senior agents each month. Your table has what that needs. 209 of your 1,200 customers churned, which gives a model enough examples to learn from. I also found no columns that give the answer away. I'm assuming two things. The senior agents will work the queue, and you'd pick from your current subscribers each month using these same columns, without the churn flag. Is that right, and roughly how many subscribers do you have in total each month? That tells me whether 500 is a small slice or a big share of them.

yeah that's right, senior agents work the queue and we'd pick from current subscribers using the same columns. I don't know the total number of subscribers each month off the top of my head, I'd have to check. is the ranking thing something i can build in sql or python or do you need a fancy tool for it?

You don't need a fancy tool for this. A basic version is a short Python script using logistic regression, and a rules-based score can be done in SQL. The harder part is checking that the ranking works on customers it hasn't seen. DCLab can do that check and give you the ranked list, so you can use that or build your own version afterward. You don't have to know your monthly subscriber total yet. It would only tell us how thin a slice of subscribers 500 is. Here are two ways to go, so pick whichever fits what you need to show your manager. Which one do you want?

It tests the model on customers it has not seen. You get: A score and rank for every subscriber, and a check of how many of the real leavers land in the top slice you'd hand to the agents, compared with picking at random.
